references.text: Psalm 23:5 mentions anointing the head with oil as a sign of hospitality and blessing: 'You anoint my head with oil'. Jesus points out that the host Simon did not anoint his head with oil, in contrast to this custom.
Psalm 141:5 mentions oil on the head as an expression of goodwill, which sheds light on the cultural background of Jesus' remark that Simon did not anoint his head.
Ecclesiastes 9:8 encourages always having oil on the head as a sign of joy and celebration. This shows that anointing with oil was a common hospitality custom that Simon neglected.

The context of the verse: The woman known as a sinner came with an alabaster jar of perfume, wept at Jesus' feet, wiped them with her hair, and anointed his feet with costly perfume – in contrast to Simon's lack of hospitality.
In Matthew 26:7, a woman anoints Jesus' head with costly perfume during the meal in Bethany. The parallel shows a similar act of anointing expressing love and devotion.
In Mark 14:3, a woman breaks an alabaster jar of pure nard oil and anoints Jesus' head. This account has thematic similarities to the anointing in Luke 7.
In John 12:3, Mary anoints Jesus' feet with costly nard perfume and wipes them with her hair, a very similar action described in Luke 7:46.
John 11:2 refers back to Mary as the one who anointed the Lord with perfume and wiped his feet with her hair, linking to the act of anointing described in Luke 7:46.
